studies.title: Systemic Allergic Reactions to mRNA COVID-19 Vaccines: A Randomized Placebo-controlled Trial.
studies.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
studies.authors: Wheatley, Lisa M, Baker, James R, Adkinson, N Franklin, Gruchalla, Rebecca et al.
studies.abstract: COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were associated in early reports with more allergic reactions than most vaccines, especially in people with allergic histories. To estimate the proportions of systemic allergic reactions to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in people reporting prior severe allergic reactions to various allergens, and/or mast cell disorders (PSAR/MCD Group) and determine if proportions are higher than in non-PSAR/non-MCD (Comparison Group). We conducted a multi-center, randomized, double-blinded (for the initial injection), placebo-controlled trial in PSAR/MCD vs Comparison adults and adolescents. Participants received a double-blinded injection with Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna COVID-19 vaccine or placebo, followed by unblinded vaccine injections. The primary outcome was the incidence of clinically-determined systemic allergic reactions within 90 minutes after injection. The trial enrolled 723 participants of a planned 3400, with 664 (56% PSAR/MCD) receiving at least one injection. Within 90 minutes of injection, systemic allergic reactions occurred in 5/180 (3%) PSAR/MCD participants given Pfizer-BioNTech (vs 0/133 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.063) and 2/173 (1%) PSAR/MCD participants given Moderna (vs 0/144 [0%] Comparison Group; p=0.27). Reactions were also reported >90 minutes and ≤48 hours only in PSAR/MCD. Among PSAR/MCD participants, reaction rates to vaccine within 90-minutes and 48-hours were similar to placebo. Extensive laboratory studies did not identify plausible reaction mechanisms. Systemic allergic reactions based solely on clinical determination within 90-minutes or 48-hours of vaccination were only observed in PSAR/MCD but failure to achieve planned enrollment limited statistical precision. Reactions to placebo and failure to identify underlying immunologic mechanisms suggest non-allergic or non-immunologic causes.

studies.title: Type I autoimmunity in chronic spontaneous urticaria: Evidence, limits, and endotype overlap.
studies.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
studies.authors: Konstantinou, George N, Grattan, Clive E H
studies.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a mast cell-driven disorder with basophil involvement and several possible upstream mechanisms. Type IIb autoimmune CSU, mediated by functional IgG autoantibodies against FcεRIα or IgE, is the best-validated endotype. Evidence for type I autoimmune (autoallergic) CSU is less complete, but findings involving IgE autoantibodies to thyroid peroxidase (TPO), IL-24, and other self-antigens suggest that IgE-dependent autoreactivity may be relevant in some patients. However, total IgE level, atopy, allergic disease, and timing of the response to omalizumab are not diagnostic of this mechanism. Rather than viewing type I and type IIb CSU as competing categories, we hypothesize 2 potentially overlapping immunologic axes: an IgE-autoantibody axis and an IgG/complement axis. Patients may lie closer to one axis, show markers of both, or remain provisionally idiopathic because current biomarkers cannot classify them with confidence. Progress will require harmonized functional assays; skin, mast cell, and basophil readouts, as well as longitudinal treatment studies. The central question is when an IgE autoantibody is only a passenger, when it is a partner, and when it is the driver of the wheal.

studies.title: [Beyond the placebo effect: exploring the mast cell-dependent analgesic effect of shallow needling control].
studies.journal: Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion
studies.authors: Luo, Zhengrong, Zhang, Youwen, Ge, Xiaolei, Tian, Xinyi et al.
studies.abstract: Based on the distribution characteristics of mast cells and existing mechanistic evidence, the study explores the potential biological effects of shallow needling control (sham-acupuncture). Regarding cellular distribution, mast cells exhibit a physiological characteristic of dense distribution in both the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, predominantly in the distal regions, and show a higher density in acupoint areas compared with non-acupoint areas. At the puncture site, shallow needling primarily targets the dermis and the superficial subcutaneous tissue, with these two layers overlapping anatomically. Regarding its mechanism of action, acupuncture can induce local mast cell degranulation through mechanical stimulation, thereby releasing bioactive substances that subsequently activate relevant signaling pathways to produce analgesic effect. The study proposes that the shallow needling control at the same acupoint or non-acupoint not merely obtains placebo effect, but also involves potential biological mechanism associated with mast cells, aiming to provide new insights for future clinical trial design and research on the underlying mechanism of acupuncture and sham-acupuncture. 基于肥大细胞的分布特点和现有机制证据，探讨浅刺对照（假针刺）的潜在生物学效应。在细胞分布上，肥大细胞具有在真皮层与皮下组织层分布密集，以远心端为主、穴位区较非穴区更为丰富的生理特点；在刺入位置上，浅刺对照主要涉及皮肤真皮层和皮下浅层，二者于解剖层面重叠。在作用机制上，针刺可通过机械刺激促使局部肥大细胞脱颗粒，释放生物活性物质，进而激活相关信号通路产生镇痛效应。提出以同穴或非穴浅刺为主的针刺对照不仅仅是安慰剂效应，还存在与肥大细胞相关的潜在生物学效应，以期为未来针刺与假针刺的临床试验设计及效应机制研究提供新的思路。.

studies.title: Luteolin alleviates neurogenic inflammation in OVA-induced combined allergic rhinitis and asthma syndrome mice through TRPV1/ERK-related signaling.
studies.journal: International archives of allergy and immunology
studies.authors: Li, Jing, Mirodilova, Firuza, Lei, Lei
studies.abstract: Combined Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma Syndrome (CARAS), a common chronic allergic respiratory disease, involves dysregulated neuro-immune interactions and neurogenic inflammation. Luteolin (LUT) has significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. However, its effects and underlying mechanism in CARAS remain unclear. This study aims to determine the effects of LUT administration during the airway challenge phase of CARAS and its association with TRPV1/ERK signaling. BALB/C mice were used to establish an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced CARAS model and LUT was administered. The nasal symptoms were evaluated by counting the number of nasal scratching and sneezing. HE and toluidine blue staining were performed to determine the histopathological changes. Total and differential cell counts in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were determined. The levels of histamine, MCP-1, substance P (SP), CGRP and Th1/Th2/Th17-related cytokines were detected by ELISA kit. Besides, TRPV1 and p-ERK expression levels were measured by immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting. Our study indicated that LUT administration significantly reduced sneezing frequency, nasal scratching behavior, and serum OVA-specific IgE level in CARAS mice compared to the model group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated that LUT administration reduced inflammatory cell accumulation and histological scores in the nasal mucosa and lung tissues and was associated with reduced inflammatory cell counts in BALF. In addition, LUT administration reduced mast cell density in both tissues. Serum histamine and MCP-1 levels and pulmonary levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-17A, and IFN-γ were also reduced following LUT administration. LUT administration also reduced serum and BALF levels of SP and CGRP. Furthermore, LUT administration reduced TRPV1 expression and p-ERK levels in the nasal mucosa and lung tissue. LUT administration attenuates allergic and inflammatory responses in OVA-induced CARAS mice, which may be associated with TRPV1/ERK signaling.

studies.title: LL-37-MRGPRX2-Mast Cell Signaling in Rosacea: Current Evidence and Directions for Human Studies.
studies.authors: Yin, Haoyang, Lu, Yiping
studies.abstract: This critical narrative review examines evidence relevant to LL-37-Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2)-mast-cell signaling in rosacea and considers the relevance of these findings to future human studies. Literature was identified through PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection searches, supplemented by examination of reference lists from relevant original studies and recent reviews. Human rosacea tissue studies show changes in mast-cell abundance or degranulation-associated staining and localize MRGPRX2 to lesional mast cells. Human mast-cell and receptor studies demonstrate LL-37-responsive MRGPRX2 calcium signaling and degranulation and show pharmacological inhibition of MRGPRX2-mediated responses. LL-37-induced mouse models support contributions of mast cells and murine Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor member B2 (MrgprB2), although human MRGPRX2 and murine MrgprB2 are pharmacologically distinct. Other LL-37-responsive pathways and downstream regulatory processes may also produce or modify similar mast-cell outcomes. Direct selective functional testing of MRGPRX2 in patients with rosacea remains lacking, and receptor-level functional findings and patient-level observations still arise largely from different study settings. Future human studies could therefore connect lesional MRGPRX2 status and selective receptor perturbation with proximal mast-cell responses and corresponding tissue or clinical changes within the same rosacea study setting. Under adequately designed study conditions, concordant findings may strengthen support for MRGPRX2 involvement, whereas partial, discordant, subgroup-restricted, or absent proximal responses may help refine its functional scope in human rosacea.

studies.title: Inducible Laryngeal Obstruction in Hypermobile Patients.
studies.authors: Menton, Stacey M, Fairweather, DeLisa, Wilson, Frances C, Zangerle, Derek J et al.
studies.abstract: To determine whether patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) have more voice, cough, swallowing, GI issues, and MC activation than patients without ILO. This retrospective study of 2162 patients meeting 2017 diagnostic criteria for hEDS (n = 507) or HSD (n = 1655) who were seen at the EDS Clinic in Mayo Clinic Florida from November 2019 to June 2025 compared patients who screened positive for ILO to those who screened negative. Patients were examined for self-reported symptoms of voice, cough, swallow, and GI issues as well as MC activation. Among patients with hEDS or HSD, 23.1% and 17.1% respectively screened positive for ILO. Patients with ILO had significantly more voice, cough, and swallow issues than patients without ILO (all p ≤ 0.007). Both diagnoses had more gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) (hEDS: 55.6% vs. 40.9%, p = 0.004; HSD: 55.8% vs. 42.2%, p < 0.0001). Additionally, both hEDS and HSD patients with ILO self-reported 18 allergy-related symptoms more often than those without ILO and had higher MC scores indicating widespread MC activation (all p < 0.0001). Cough, dysphagia, and elevated MC score were statistically significant predictors of ILO in both hEDS and HSD within a logistic regression analysis. Chronic cough, dysphagia, and elevated MC symptom burden were the strongest independent predictors of ILO across both hEDS and HSD, underscoring the need for routine multidisciplinary laryngeal assessment in this population.

studies.title: Food-Associated Kounis Syndrome: Clinical Spectrum and Diagnostic Considerations from a Case Report and Systematic Qualitative Synthesis of Published Cases.
studies.authors: Sanchez-Fernandez, Sergio, Lasarte, Gabriel Gastaminza, Garófalo, Carmen D'Amelio, Paredes-Gutierrez, Enrique et al.
studies.abstract: Kounis syndrome (KS) is a hypersensitivity-associated acute coronary syndrome. Food-associated KS remains poorly characterized, and its clinical presentation may be mimicked by non-immune food-related toxic reactions. To characterize the food exposures, clinical and cardiovascular presentations, allergological assessment, potential cofactors, KS phenotypes, management, and outcomes reported in food-associated KS. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to August 22, 2026. Original case reports, case series, and sufficiently informative conference reports describing objective coronary involvement temporally associated with a food or food-derived exposure were included. Patient-level data were synthesized qualitatively. KS diagnostic certainty, coronary phenotype, food causality, and presumed mechanism were assessed separately. Planned sensitivity analyses restricted the synthesis to confirmed or suspected food allergy, definite or probable KS, and cases without epinephrine administration before coronary onset or its first objective documentation. The synthesis included 50 publications or reports describing 53 unique patients. Food-related mechanisms comprised confirmed food allergy in 20 patients, clinically suspected food allergy in 26, scombroid poisoning in six, and a Coprinopsis atramentaria-alcohol interaction in one. The reported coronary spectrum ranged from transient vasospasm and nonobstructive presentations to plaque-related myocardial infarction, native-coronary thrombosis, and stent or graft thrombosis. Type I was the most frequently assigned phenotype. Allergological assessment, paired acute and baseline tryptase measurements, treatment chronology, and long-term follow-up were inconsistently reported. The main cardiovascular patterns remained broadly consistent across the planned sensitivity analyses. Food-associated KS encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of allergic coronary presentations. Clinically similar non-immune food-related toxic reactions, including scombroid poisoning, should be recognized as differential diagnoses and analyzed separately from true allergic KS. Diagnosis requires integration of exposure chronology, objective cardiovascular findings, coronary substrate, allergological evidence, potential cofactors, and competing exposures. Intramuscular epinephrine remains the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, and temporal precedence should not be interpreted as evidence that epinephrine caused the coronary event.

studies.title: Mast cell activation syndrome: Global perspectives from a World Allergy Organization survey on knowledge, diagnosis, and access to care.
studies.authors: Giavina-Bianchi, Pedro, Giavina-Bianchi, Mara, Morais-Almeida, Mário, Álvarez-Twose, Iván et al.
studies.abstract: Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) has emerged as a highly debated and increasingly recognized condition in allergy and clinical immunology. Despite established AIM/ECNM consensus criteria, major uncertainties persist regarding its diagnosis, implementation in real-world practice, and equitable access to diagnostic resources worldwide. To evaluate global knowledge, diagnostic practices, clinical exposure, and access to care related to MCAS among allergists and clinical immunologists, and to identify critical unmet needs contributing to diagnostic uncertainty. We conducted a cross-sectional international survey primarily involving allergists and clinical immunologists affiliated with the World Allergy Organization (WAO). The survey instrument was developed by international experts in mast cell disorders, including contributors to the conceptual framework and consensus diagnostic criteria for MCAS. The questionnaire assessed knowledge of consensus diagnostic criteria, clinical experience with suspected and confirmed MCAS, access to validated laboratory testing, diagnostic confidence, and treatment strategies. Regional comparisons were performed to identify disparities in practice patterns and resource availability. Marked global heterogeneity was observed in knowledge of MCAS diagnostic criteria, application of consensus frameworks, and access to essential laboratory testing. Across all regions, clinicians reported a substantial and consistent gap between the number of patients suspected of having MCAS and those who ultimately fulfilled all diagnostic criteria. Objective biomarker confirmation-particularly documentation of dynamic serum tryptase changes and access to urinary mast cell mediator metabolites-emerged as the principal diagnostic bottleneck worldwide. However, the imbalance between suspected and confirmed cases persisted even in regions with relatively greater laboratory access, suggesting that structural limitations coexist with potential diagnostic overextension and inconsistent clinical phenotyping. Management approaches were predominantly empiric and symptom-driven, often implemented in the absence of complete diagnostic confirmation. Respondents highlighted the need for clearer guidance, improved biomarker accessibility, and refinement of definitions to reduce diagnostic ambiguity. MCAS represents a condition in which both under-recognition and diagnostic uncertainty remain important challenges in contemporary practice. Significant unmet needs include strengthening clinician knowledge and application of the AIM/ECNM diagnostic framework, expanding global access to validated biomarkers, improving diagnostic precision, and harmonizing clinical approaches. At the same time, the findings of this survey suggest a need for continued evaluation and refinement of the current diagnostic framework to improve its applicability across the heterogeneous clinical spectrum of patients with suspected MCAS. Coordinated international efforts are urgently required to reduce diagnostic uncertainty, minimize inequities in care, and support the continued evolution toward a more accurate, consistent, and clinically applicable diagnostic approach worldwide.

studies.title: Imperatorin exerts anti-colorectal cancer effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell degranulation.
studies.journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
studies.authors: Shi, Xianpeng, Zhang, Peng, Cui, Xia, Hou, Yajing et al.
studies.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major global malignancy with a poor prognosis in advanced stages. Aberrant mast cell activation within the tumor microenvironment (TME) drives CRC progression; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumor-promoting role of mast cells in the hypoxic TME remain unclear, and effective therapies targeting these cells are lacking. To investigate the role of the NADPH oxidase 2 (NOX2)-reactive oxygen species (ROS)-calcium signaling axis in mast cell activation and evaluate the anti-CRC activity of imperatorin (IMP), a natural furanocoumarin. Human mast cell and CRC cell lines were used to establish hypoxic activation and conditioned medium co-culture systems. Tissue microarrays, single‑cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets and CT26 allograft mouse models were employed, combined with gain/loss-of-function, Western Blot, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence and cell functional assays. NOX2 expression was significantly upregulated in activated mast cells from human CRC tissues. IMP inhibited NOX2, thereby blocking hypoxia-induced oxidative stress and mast cell degranulation. This intervention suppressed the secretion of tumor-promoting mediators and effectively inhibited CRC cell proliferation and invasion. Furthermore, in vivo experiments demonstrated that IMP dose-dependently suppressed CRC allograft growth in murine models without causing overt systemic toxicity. This study reveals a mechanism by which mast cells promote CRC progression in the hypoxic TME and demonstrates that IMP exerts potent anti-CRC effects by targeting NOX2 to inhibit mast cell activation. These findings identify both a therapeutic target and a promising lead compound for TME-targeted CRC therapy.

studies.title: Mechanistic insight into eosinophilic enteritis and related disorders.
studies.authors: Syverson, Erin P, Venkatesh, Rajitha D, Bailey, Dominique D
studies.abstract: Eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases (EGIDs) affecting the gastrointestinal tract outside of the esophagus are categorized as non-EoE EGIDs, and knowledge regarding their natural history and pathophysiology is rapidly advancing. This review synthesizes evolving mechanistic insights in non-EoE EGID immunopathogenesis, emerging paradigms of disease development, and how these insights influence potential therapeutic options for these conditions. The prevalence of non-EoE EGIDs is rising, though overall prevalence remains much lower than that of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). Recent standardization of the nomenclature and histologic diagnostic thresholds for non-EoE EGIDs has facilitated progress in understanding the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and therapeutic targets of these conditions. Transcriptomic signatures of disease in the proximal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, and small intestine, are distinct from those in the colon, suggesting that segment-specific therapeutics may be appropriate. Mechanisms beyond eosinophilic inflammation, including mast cell activation, Th2 cytokine signaling, and structural remodeling, may also contribute to disease pathogenesis. Mechanistic insights elucidated from extensive transcriptomic studies and clinical trials have revealed the broader type 2 pathophysiology of non-EoE EGIDs, thereby offering a valuable opportunity to identify novel therapeutic targets and inform the design of future clinical trials.

studies.title: The dual and context-dependent role of mast cells in cutaneous wound healing and scar formation.
studies.authors: Kushwaha, Pooja, Mukhopadhyay, Sangita
studies.abstract: Successful tissue repair depends on the precise orchestration of phase-specific cellular responses alongside sustained activity of multifunctional immune regulators. Mast cells, which have primarily been long regarded as effector cells of allergic reactions, have emerged as pivotal modulators of wound repair. Importantly, mast cell activity exhibits a dual nature: while transient activation supports efficient repair and granulation tissue formation, sustained or excessive activation is associated with pathological fibrosis, hypertrophic scarring and keloid formation. Although many experimental studies and clinical evidences implicate a critical role for mast cells in wound repair, several key questions remain. Specifically, the contributions of distinct mast cell subtypes and the precise temporal dynamics of their mediator release, as well as the intricate molecular crosstalk between mast cells, stromal components, and other infiltrating immune cells remans a subject of active investigation. This review highlights current literature on the multifaceted roles of mast cells across the successive phases of wound-healing, and the specific mechanisms by which mast cells support or impair tissue repair, outlining unresolved questions in the field. Through this discussion, we aim to provide a framework for developing new therapeutic strategies to improve healing outcomes and facilitate better scar management.

studies.title: Mast cell degranulation damages glymphatic system via PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 to exacerbate hydrocephalus post intraventricular hemorrhage.
studies.authors: Yang, Yijian, Ouyang, Qian, Wang, Junqiang, Wang, Kaiyue et al.
studies.abstract: Hydrocephalus following intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) remains a serious neurological condition with limited treatment options beyond invasive surgical interventions, underscoring the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence implicates impaired glymphatic system function in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus, particularly through dysregulation of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expression in astrocytes, which is essential for cerebral waste clearance and fluid homeostasis. Since mast cells are key mediators of neuroinflammation and can influence cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics, this study investigated their role and underlying mechanisms in hydrocephalus following IVH. An IVH model was established in male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats by injecting autologous blood into the lateral ventricle. Rats were divided into the following groups: sham operation, IVH, IVH treated with the mast cell stabilizer disodium cromoglycate (DSCG), and IVH treated with DSCG plus the protein kinase C (PKC) activator phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA). In a rat model of IVH, mast cell degranulation and the release of tryptase and chymase were observed, accompanied by significant impairment of glymphatic influx and efflux. This dysfunction was characterized by reduced penetration of CSF tracers into the brain parenchyma and diminished clearance of interstitial solutes. Pharmacological stabilization of mast cells with DSCG substantially improved glymphatic function, restored glymphatic structural integrity, reduced ventricular enlargement, and ameliorated neurological deficits. Mechanistically, mast cell-derived proteases activated the PKC/p38MAPK signaling pathway, leading to decreased AQP4 expression and altered AQP4 distribution at astrocytic endfeet, thereby disrupting the perivascular polarization critical for glymphatic flow. This mechanism was supported by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), which demonstrated an interaction between p38MAPK and AQP4, and by rescue experiments, which showed that PKC activation reversed DSCG's protective effects. In vitro experiments conducted under indirect co-culture conditions further demonstrated the interaction between mast cells and astrocytes. Our results reveal a novel mast cell-PKC/p38MAPK/AQP4 pathway in the development of hydrocephalus following IVH and identify mast cell stabilization as a promising therapeutic strategy for hydrocephalus post-IVH, offering a potential non-invasive approach to manage this devastating complication.

studies.title: From nasal cytology to cellular endotyping: mast cell-eosinophil interactions and overlapping inflammation in allergic rhinitis.
studies.authors: Gelardi, Matteo
studies.abstract: Allergic rhinitis is traditionally defined by allergen sensitization and type 2 inflammation, yet increasing evidence indicates that this framework does not fully capture the biological heterogeneity of the nasal mucosa. The local inflammatory landscape reflects a dynamic interaction among epithelial cells, innate and adaptive lymphoid populations, mast cells, eosinophils, stromal elements, and vascular components, and may diverge substantially from systemic biomarkers. Recent single-cell and multi-omic studies have further revealed disease-associated alterations in epithelial differentiation, stromal activation, and cell-cell communication, reinforcing the concept of the nasal mucosa as an integrated immunological ecosystem. Within this context, mast cell-eosinophil interactions appear particularly relevant, as their coexistence and degranulation may characterize inflammatory states that differ from isolated eosinophilia. Nasal cytology provides a clinically accessible morphological readout of this local cellular architecture and has shown that allergic rhinitis does not correspond to a single cytological expression. In some patients, established allergic sensitization coexists with recognized non-allergic cellular rhinitis entities, including non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophils (NARES), non-allergic rhinitis with mast cells (NARMA), and non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophils and mast cells (NARESMA), giving rise to the concept of overlapping rhinitis. This phenomenon challenges a binary allergic versus non-allergic classification and may contribute to difficult-to-treat disease and incomplete therapeutic responses. Although these nosological entities are clinically and cytologically defined, they should not be considered synonymous with molecular endotypes. Their future value may instead lie in a cytology-informed endotyping strategy integrating morphology with local biomarkers, proteomics, transcriptomics, and single-cell approaches. This Review discusses the cellular players and interactions shaping allergic rhinitis, the biological and clinical relevance of overlapping inflammation, and the potential role of nasal cytology as an interface between clinical phenotyping and molecular endotyping.

studies.title: Tryptase Locus Variation Contributes to Normal-Range Basal Serum Tryptase Variability and Is Associated With Anaphylaxis.
studies.journal: Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology
studies.authors: Svetina, Manca, Lyons, Jonathan J, Kopač, Peter, Šelb, Julij et al.
studies.abstract: Increased basal serum tryptase level (BST) is associated with anaphylaxis. In the absence of clonal mast cell disease and hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT), the contribution of the tryptase locus variation to BST and anaphylaxis remains undefined. To determine the impact of tryptase locus variation on BST and anaphylaxis. Individuals with systemic Hymenoptera venom allergic reactions, large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization underwent a novel ddPCR-based tryptase genotyping to quantify active tryptase alleles. Individuals positive for KIT p.D816V or HαT were excluded. The cohort consisted of 295 individuals with systemic reactions, 140 with large local reactions, and 29 asymptomatically sensitized individuals. Active tryptase allele number, excluding the inactive βIIIFS allele, correlated with BST levels (r = 0.34, p < 0.0001); all BST values were within the normal range. Patients with systemic reactions had higher BST compared with those with large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization (median, 4.5 ng/mL vs. 3.5 ng/mL; p < 0.0001). Individuals carrying four active β-tryptase alleles were less likely to experience anaphylaxis than those carrying two or three active β-tryptase alleles (26.7% vs. 42.3%; p = 0.024). A trend towards more severe reactions was observed in individuals carrying α-tryptase allele together with a higher number of active β-tryptase alleles. Variation at the tryptase locus explains differences in BST levels within the normal range. Four active β-tryptase alleles were associated with a lower frequency of anaphylaxis.

studies.title: Insulin Enhances Nitroglycerin-Induced Hyperalgesia Through Insulin-Responsive Receptor Signalling Involving the Trigeminovascular System and Meningeal Mast Cells.
studies.authors: Torun, Ibrahim Ethem, Celik, Humeyra, Kilinc, Erkan, Kurtoglu, Muhammet Guzel
studies.abstract: Migraine headache prevalence is lower in patients with diabetes, but the underlying mechanisms remains unclear. This study explored the influences of hyperglycemia, insulin and insulin receptor (IR)/insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R)-related signalling on migraine-related mechanisms in in vivo and ex vivo rat models. In in vivo experiments, migraine-relevant responses were induced by systemic injection of nitroglycerin (NTG), whereas hyperglycemia was induced by streptozotocin (STZ). The effects of hyperglycemia, insulin and the dual IR/IGF-1R inhibitor BMS-754807 were investigated. In ex vivo experiments, the effects of insulin and BMS on basal and capsaicin-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) releases from migraine-associated tissues (peripheral meningeal afferents and trigeminal ganglion, and central brainstem trigeminal nucleus) were directly tested. Mechanical hyperalgesia was evaluated by von-Frey, CGRP and c-Fos levels by ELISA and meningeal mast cells by toluidine-blue staining. In in vivo NTG group, insulin further lowered the pain threshold and further enhanced CGRP and c-fos concentrations in trigeminal tissues and mast cell activation in the meninges. Hyperglycemia alone or in the NTG-treated group did not change these parameters. In ex vivo experiments, direct administration of insulin stimulated CGRP release in meningeal and trigeminal ganglion, but not trigeminal nucleus, tissues and further enhanced capsaicin-stimulated CGRP release, confirming the in vivo effects. The in vivo and ex vivo effects of insulin were reversed by BMS. Hyperglycemia did not modify the NTG-induced responses. However, insulin facilitates migraine-related responses by enhancing trigeminal CGRP signalling and meningeal mast cell activation through IR and/or IGF-1R-related signalling. Modulation of insulin-responsive IR/IGF-1R-related signalling within the trigeminovascular system may represent a potential target for future therapeutic strategies.

studies.title: Gut inflammation favors adverse food reactions by disrupting the microbial metabolism of food triggers.
studies.authors: Da Luz, Bruna B, Rondeau, Liam E, Dang, Rebecca, Coppens, Dana et al.
studies.abstract: We sensitized mice to different foods (dairy and gluten) after intestinal inflammation (chemically- and hapten-induced models), then mice were re-exposed to the sensitizing foods through diet enrichment. To study whether inflamed microbiota facilitates adverse food reactions, we employed gnotobiotic models and bacterial supplementation experiments. We assessed markers of intestinal inflammation and sensitization, clinical responses, RNA transcripts, and microbiota composition and function. In a translational approach, we recruited IBD patients in remission and healthy controls, recorded self-reported food intolerances and clinical responses to triggering foods, and collected feces for gut microbiota analyses. Intestinal inflammation facilitates food sensitization by disrupting microbial antigen metabolism, recruiting mast cells to the colon, and favoring IgE production. In gnotobiotic models, inflammation-driven depletion of colonic bacteria involved in food digestion contributed to food sensitization. Upon re-exposure to triggering foods, sensitized mice experienced visceral pain and low-grade inflammation through mast-cell mediated mechanisms, which also worsened experimental colitis. Supplementation with depleted bacteria or treatment with mast cell stabilizers attenuated food-driven responses. In IBD patients, self-reported food intolerances were common and associated with microbial disruption and depletion of food-metabolizing bacteria. Microbial metabolism of foods is disrupted after intestinal inflammation. This facilitates food sensitization, through colonic mast cell-mediated immune responses, which may explain the high number of adverse food reactions reported by IBD patients.

studies.title: IL-18-associated basophil and mast cell activation in sepsis.
studies.journal: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
studies.authors: Wang, Junling, Qin, Bingyu, Zhang, Xueyan, Zhan, Mengmeng et al.
studies.abstract: The contributions of basophils and mast cells to sepsis immunopathology remains poorly understood. Interleukin-18 (IL-18) has established roles in innate immune activation, but its relationships with basophil and mast cell activation during sepsis have not been fully defined. We investigated expression of IL-18Rα and activation marker CD63 on blood basophils of patients with sepsis using flow cytometry and RNA-sequencing. Sepsis mouse model and human cell lines were used to assess the effect of IL-18 on basophil and mast cell activation. Close correlations between elevated plasma IL-18 level and increased CD63, IL-18Rα and IL-18Rβ protein expression on basophils of patients with sepsis were observed. Transcriptomic analysis revealed extensive reprogramming of septic basophils, including upregulation of CD63 and IL18RAP, together with enrichment of pathways related to ribosome biogenesis, mitochondrial translation, oxidative phosphorylation, proteasome, DNA replication and cell cycle. Furthermore, we observed increased expression of CD63 and IL-18Rα on basophils and mast cells in septic mice, and IL-18 upregulated their expression and mast cell accumulation in both healthy and septic mice. Additionally, elevated plasma and peritoneal levels of IL-18, IL-5, CCL2 and tryptase were observed in septic mice. In vitro experiments demonstrated that both IL-18 and plasma from patients with sepsis induced upregulation of CD63 and IL-18Rα on KU812 and HMC-1 cell lines. Collectively, our findings suggest that IL-18-associated basophil and mast cell activation may participate in sepsis-related inflammation.

studies.title: Ketotifen attenuates paraquat-induced nephrotoxicity in mice
studies.authors: Vadizadeh, Ali, Badiee, Mahdieh Sadat, Rahmani, Ali Hasan, Mahdavinia, Masoud et al.
studies.abstract: Paraquat (PQ) is a toxic herbicide to humans and animals that causes kidney damage. Ketotifen (KTF) is a first-generation antihistamine and a potent mast cell stabilizer with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This study aimed to evaluate the protective effect of KTF against PQ-induced nephrotoxicity in mice by suppressing inflammation, oxidative stress, and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). Thirty-five male NMRI mice were randomly divided into 5 groups (n = 7) as follows: control group receiving normal saline as vehicle (10 mL/kg/day, IP), KTF, PQ, PQ + KTF 2, and PQ + KTF 4 groups. PQ was administered as a single dose (30 mg/kg, IP) on day 4. The mice received KTF at the doses of 2 and 4 mg/kg/day, IP, for seven days. On the eighth day of the study, the mice were anesthetized, and their kidneys were removed. Then, oxidative stress and inflammation factors and iNOS protein expression were evaluated, and histological examinations were performed. KTF resulted in a significant decrease in blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, thiobarbituric acid-reactive substances, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and iNOS protein expression, and a significant increase in albumin, total thiol, and the activity of antioxidant enzymes including catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase in PQ-induced nephrotoxicity compared with the PQ group, which were confirmed by histopathological findings. The results of this study showed that KTF could improve PQ-induced renal injury in mice by reducing oxidative stress, inflammation, and iNOS protein expression.

studies.title: The Role of Mast Cells and Their Potential as a Therapeutic Target For Neuroinflammation.
studies.authors: Scuderi, Sarah Adriana, Basilotta, Rossella, Cucinotta, Laura, Ardizzone, Alessio et al.
studies.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as a central mechanism underlying the onset and progression of numerous neurological disorders, including neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and cerebrovascular diseases. Although microglia and astrocytes are traditionally considered the primary mediators of inflammatory responses within the central nervous system (CNS), accumulating evidence has identified mast cells (MCs) as important contributors to neuroimmune regulation. Strategically located at the interface between the peripheral immune system and the CNS, MCs can rapidly respond to a variety of endogenous and exogenous stimuli through the release of bioactive mediators, including histamine, proteases, cytokines, chemokines, and lipid-derived molecules. These mediators influence blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, promote glial activation, modulate neuronal signaling, and contribute to the amplification of inflammatory cascades. Increasing experimental and clinical evidence supports the involvement of MCs in the pathogenesis of several neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, migraine, and ischemic brain injury. Consequently, modulation of mast cell activity has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for limiting neuroinflammatory damage and restoring neuroimmune homeostasis. This review provides an overview of mast cell biology within the CNS, discusses the molecular mechanisms linking MCs to neuroinflammation, examines their contribution to major neurological disorders, and highlights current and emerging therapeutic strategies targeting MCs-mediated pathways. A deeper understanding of mast cell functions in neuroinflammatory processes may facilitate the development of innovative and more effective interventions for neurological diseases.

studies.title: A Biotinylated Heptapeptide Containing a D-Amino Acid Suppresses Both IgE-Dependent and -Independent Allergic Edema in Mice.
studies.authors: Ohira, Makoto, Yuki, Hana, Tsumuraya, Miu, Nozaki, Erika et al.
studies.abstract: We previously found that, among three biotinylated heptapeptides (Peptide 1, Peptide 2, and Peptide 3) derived from the amino acid sequence of Asp-hemolysin, a protein toxin produced by Aspergillus fumigatus, Peptide 2, which contains a d-amino acid, exhibits potent anti-allergic activity in vitro and in vivo. In this study, we evaluated the effects of Peptide 2 on immunoglobulin E (IgE)-dependent allergic edema induced by ovalbumin (OVA) in OVA-specific IgE transgenic mice, IgE-independent allergic edema induced by compound 48/80 (C48/80), and nonallergic inflammatory edema induced by histamine, serotonin, bradykinin, zymosan A, and λ-carrageenan. Peptide 2 significantly suppressed both OVA-IgE- and C48/80-induced paw edema, indicating inhibitory effects on both IgE-dependent and -independent allergic responses. Peptide 2 also dose-dependently inhibited histamine-induced edema but did not affect serotonin-, bradykinin-, zymosan A-, or λ-carrageenan-induced edema. These findings indicate that Peptide 2 modulates IgE-dependent and -independent allergic responses involving mast cell activation and histamine-related pathways and may be a candidate for the development of selective anti-allergic agents.

studies.title: CHRONIC URTICARIA AND LEAD EXPOSURE: EVALUATION OF IMMUNOLOGICAL MARKERS.
studies.authors: Shavlakadze, N, Phkhakadze, I, Silagadze, A, Kobuladze, D et al.
studies.abstract: Chronic urticaria (CU) is a mast-cell-driven disorder involving inflammatory and autoimmune mechanisms. Lead can affect immune function, but its relationship with CU has been little studied. To examine the association of blood lead levels (BLLs) with CU, active wheals at blood sampling, and selected immunological markers. This single-center case-control study included 303 participants from Western Georgia: 211 patients with CU and 92 healthy controls. BLLs were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Eosinophils, total IgE, histamine, anti-IgE autoantibodies, and FcεRIα autoantibodies were assessed. BLL ≥10 µg/dL was used as the predefined analytical threshold for higher lead exposure. Associations were evaluated using group comparisons, Spearman correlation, and age-adjusted regression analyses. BLLs were higher in patients with CU than in healthy controls. BLL ≥10 µg/dL was present in 66.8% of patients and 33.7% of controls (OR 3.96; 95% CI 2.36-6.66; p<0.001), and the association remained significant after adjustment for age (aOR 4.07; 95% CI 2.38-6.96; p<0.001). Within the CU group, higher BLLs were associated with eosinophilia and higher histamine, anti-IgE, and FcεRIα autoantibody levels, but not with total IgE. BLL ≥10 µg/dL was also associated with active wheals at blood sampling after adjustment for age (aOR 3.36; 95% CI 1.75-6.45; p<0.001). In an exploratory analysis, the dual-positive anti-IgE/FcεRIα group had the highest frequencies of BLL ≥10 µg/dL (83.3%) and active wheals (92.4%). Compared with patients in whom neither autoantibody was elevated, the dual-positive group had the strongest age-adjusted association with BLL ≥10 µg/dL (aOR 5.49; 95% CI 2.38-12.70; p<0.001). Patients with CU had higher BLLs than healthy controls. Within the CU group, higher BLLs were associated with eosinophilia, histamine, anti-IgE and FcεRIα autoantibodies, and active wheals, but not with total IgE. These associations require confirmation in prospective studies.

studies.title: Bridging immune activation and neural regulation: exploring anaphylaxis through the neuroimmunological lens.
studies.authors: Malkaza, A, Makris, M, Xepapadaki, P, Papadopoulos, N G
studies.abstract: Anaphylaxis is an acute, potentially fatal systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by striking variability in onset and severity. Although it is traditionally attributed to IgE-mediated activation of mast cells and basophils, multiple IgE-independent pathways are increasingly recognized, including IgG-mediated mechanisms, MRGPRX2-dependent mast-cell activation, and complement-derived anaphylatoxin signaling. Beyond the immune mechanisms, accumulating experimental evidence suggests that neuronal circuits may participate early and contribute to disease severity. In this narrative review, we synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence supporting a receptor-level framework in which mast-cell mediators and proteases activate and sensitize TRPV1/TRPA1-expressing sensory neurons through protease-activated receptor (PAR) signaling. Subsequent neuronal activation can trigger the release of neuropeptides, including substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which may contribute to vascular leakage and systemic manifestations while further amplifying mast-cell activation, including through MRGPRX2. Together, these interactions support the concept of a self-reinforcing neuroimmune amplification loop that may help explain the rapid onset and clinical heterogeneity of anaphylaxis. We propose this framework as a conceptual model to integrate current evidence, highlight potential adjunct therapeutic strategies beyond epinephrine, and identify key priorities for future translational and clinical research while acknowledging the current limitations of human evidence.

studies.title: Under the Drapes: Unmasking the Mechanisms and Clinical Diagnosis of Perioperative Hypersensitivity.
studies.authors: Ebo, Didier G, Peeters, Laura, Toscano, Alessandro, Elst, Jessy et al.
studies.abstract: Perioperative hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon but potentially life-threatening complications of anaesthesia and remain a major concern in clinical practice. This review provides an updated overview of the mechanisms and aetiologies underlying perioperative hypersensitivity and examines contemporary diagnostic strategies for identifying the responsible agent. Emphasis is placed on the integration of clinical assessment with laboratory and functional testing to establish an accurate diagnosis and guide the selection of safe alternatives for subsequent anaesthetic procedures. Current evidence is complemented by the authors' extensive clinical experience in the field. Recent advances have highlighted the complexity of perioperative hypersensitivity, encompassing both antigen-dependent and non-antigen-dependent mechanisms. Neuromuscular blocking agents, antibiotics, latex, and chlorhexidine remain among the most frequently implicated triggers, underscoring the importance of a systematic and comprehensive evaluation. A stepwise diagnostic strategy integrating in vitro assays, skin testing, basophil and mast cell activation tests, and, in selected cases, drug provocation testing can improve identification of the culprit agent and assessment of alternative drugs. The complementary use of these approaches, interpreted within the clinical context, is particularly important when conventional testing yields inconclusive results. Accurate identification of the cause of perioperative hypersensitivity is critical to preventing recurrent, potentially fatal reactions and ensuring safe future anaesthetic care. A structured diagnostic approach that combines detailed clinical evaluation with targeted immunological and functional testing enables individualised risk assessment and informed selection of alternative agents. Incorporating current evidence with clinical expertise can therefore optimise diagnostic accuracy and strengthen strategies for the prevention of recurrent perioperative hypersensitivity.

studies.title: Eosinophil-Mast Cell Inflammation in Middle Ear Effusion Associated With Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps.
studies.authors: Gelardi, Matteo, Chiappinelli, Adriano, Maselli Del Giudice, Alessandro, Cassano, Michele
studies.abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is predominantly associated with type 2 inflammation, although the inflammatory profile may involve both eosinophils and mast cells. Middle ear disease in CRSwNP is usually attributed to Eustachian tube dysfunction, but inflammatory involvement of the middle ear may also occur. We report the cytological evaluation of middle ear effusion from a patient with CRSwNP. May-Grünwald-Giemsa staining revealed eosinophils, mast cells, and extracellular granules consistent with degranulation. The simultaneous presence of these cellular components suggests an active type 2 inflammatory microenvironment rather than a purely mechanical or obstructive effusion. This observation supports the hypothesis that, in selected patients with CRSwNP, middle ear involvement may represent an extension of the sinonasal inflammatory process. Cytological assessment may therefore provide additional information for inflammatory phenotyping of middle ear disease associated with CRSwNP.

studies.title: The trigger-timing framework for long COVID: using symptom triggers and temporal patterns to guide mechanistic stratification and treatment planning.
studies.authors: Groysman, Robert
studies.abstract: Long COVID is characterized by substantial clinical heterogeneity, with similar symptoms often arising from different underlying physiological mechanisms. Fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, palpitations, dyspnea, gastrointestinal symptoms, sleep disruption, and exertional intolerance may each reflect autonomic dysfunction, mitochondrial or bioenergetic impairment, endothelial or microvascular dysfunction, mast cell or histamine-mediated signaling, gut dysbiosis, neuroendocrine dysregulation, or interactions among these domains. Symptom-based classification alone may therefore be insufficient for identifying dominant mechanisms or guiding treatment selection. This manuscript proposes the trigger-timing framework as a clinically accessible, hypothesis-generating method for translating patient-reported symptom behavior into mechanism-informed interpretation. The framework is based on the premise that common daily stressors, including upright posture, temperature exposure, physical or cognitive exertion, meals, emotional stress, sleep disruption, alcohol exposure, and intercurrent illness, function as real-world physiologic probes. The timing of symptom worsening after these stressors provides additional information because immediate, short-delay, same-day, delayed, cumulative, and circadian responses may reflect different response kinetics. The framework integrates four core clinical dimensions: the trigger that provokes symptom worsening, the timing of symptom onset, the symptom pattern that emerges, and the relief or recovery pattern that follows. Immediate worsening with standing, heat exposure, meals, or upright exertion, especially when relieved by lying down, supports an autonomic or circulatory pattern. Delayed worsening after physical or cognitive exertion supports impaired recovery physiology and post-exertional malaise. Meal-related symptoms may suggest autonomic, metabolic, gastrointestinal, or mast cell-related physiology depending on timing and accompanying symptoms. Circadian or persistent patterns may suggest neuroendocrine, sleep-related, autonomic, or inflammatory rhythm instability. This framework is intended as a companion operational framework to a mechanism-anchored network model of Long COVID. It may help guide targeted diagnostic evaluation, treatment prioritization, sequencing decisions, longitudinal tracking, and research cohort enrichment. The model remains conceptual and requires prospective validation to determine whether trigger-timing patterns correlate with objective physiological measures, predict differential treatment response, and improve outcomes compared with symptom-based stratification alone.

studies.title: Material basis and MRGPRB3-associated mechanisms of dictamni cortex against pseudo-allergic reactions.
studies.authors: Zhao, Huan, Yue, Lu, Zhu, Meiyin, Long, Ziyu et al.
studies.abstract: Dictamni Cortex (BXP), derived from the dried root bark of Dictamnus dasycarpus Turcz., is a traditional herbal medicine widely recognized for its anti-inflammatory and anti-allergic properties, particularly in treating skin diseases.Although BXP inhibits mast cell degranulation, its regulatory effects on the pseudo-allergy receptor MRGPRB3 and its primary blood-absorbed active components remain unclear. This study investigated the in vivo protective effects of BXP against pseudo-allergic reactions, identified its absorbed constituents, and evaluated their effects on MRGPRB3-associated mast-cell activation in vitro. Compound 48/80 (C48/80) was used to establish local pseudo-allergic, systemic pseudo-allergic, pruritus, and RBL-2H3 cell degranulation models. UPLC-Q-TOF/MS was used to identify absorbed constituents in BXP-containing serum. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were used to screen and evaluate potential MRGPRB3-associated active constituents, followed by functional validation using siRNA-mediated Mrgprb3 knockdown. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) assays in HEK293 cells expressing human MRGPRX2 were used to explore the effects of these constituents on MRGPRX2-associated G-protein signaling. In vivo, BXP reduced C48/80-induced dorsal skin vascular leakage, paw swelling, Evans blue extravasation, systemic hypothermia, and scratching behavior. BXP also alleviated skin histopathological damage and decreased serum monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), histamine, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels.
